description: Curated golden questions for the Intel MKL Python extension packages (mkl_fft, mkl_random, mkl_umath). Each item is verified against upstream source and selected for discriminating power: a knowledgeable agent should score differently from one producing fluent but unsourced advice. The set measures whether an agent decides fit correctly from the code, reports honest NOs, activates the extensions with real API names, proves activation reliably, and declines to invent performance numbers.
version_or_doc_snapshot: Verified against upstream source for IntelPython/mkl_fft, mkl_random, and mkl_umath, then revalidated question-by-question by independent per-persona review. Difficulty reflects that review rather than an initial guess. Eligibility thresholds cited in expected_topics are private #defines in mkl_umath, not published API, and may change between releases; treat them as read-from-source facts, and re-read them from the installed build before relying on a specific number.

questions.text: A hot loop calls `np.sin(a)` where `a = base.T` and `base` is a C-contiguous `(1000, 4)` float64 array, so `a` is a transposed view of shape `(4, 1000)` holding 4000 elements. Would patching mkl_umath accelerate this call? Explain precisely what decides it.
expected_topics: No, but not because of contiguity. `.T` of a 2-D C-contiguous array is exactly F-contiguous, so NumPy's iterator coalesces both axes into a single run with `steps[0] == sizeof(double)`. `IS_UNARY_CONT` and therefore `can_vectorize` both PASS.
The gate `can_vectorize && dimensions[0] > VML_TRANSCEDENTAL_THRESHOLD` fails purely on size: the coalesced inner-loop length is 4000, and the threshold is 8192 (strict `>`).

`dimensions[0]` is the inner-loop length after coalescing, not the array's shape. Scale the same expression up and it does dispatch: `np.ones((1_000_000, 4)).T` gives `dimensions[0] == 4000000` and reaches VML.

Judge the call site on `steps[]` and the coalesced run length, not on `.T` and not on the C_CONTIGUOUS flag. A genuinely strided view (`a[::2]`, `a[:, ::2]`) is buffered into chunks capped at NumPy's buffer size, which matches the transcendental threshold, so the strict `>` comparison is never satisfied and the VML kernel is not reached. Copy to contiguous first if dispatch is needed.

metadata.expected_workflow: eligibility gate check before recommending a patch
metadata.why_it_matters: Tests whether the agent reasons from strides and the coalesced inner-loop length rather than assuming `.T` implies non-contiguous. The plausible wrong answer reaches the right verdict for the wrong reason.

questions.text: A signal-processing module runs `np.exp`, `np.log`, and `np.tanh` over large contiguous `complex128` arrays. Which MKL extension helps, and why or why not?
expected_topics: mkl_umath does not help. `exp`, `log`, `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt`, and `tanh` ship float32/float64 loops only (`f->f`, `d->d`); patching installs nothing for complex input.
Results for complex input stay bit-identical to stock NumPy because patching is signature-matched (`PyUFunc_ReplaceLoopBySignature`) and no complex loop exists to substitute for these ufuncs.

Complex loops exist for elementwise arithmetic, comparison, and predicate ufuncs (add, subtract, multiply, divide, conjugate, square, reciprocal, sign, fmax/fmin, the six comparisons, isfinite/isinf/isnan, the logical ops) -- none of them transcendental. `absolute` takes complex input but returns real (`F->f`, `D->d`). Do not present the complex-capable set as a short list.
If the module also performs FFTs, mkl_fft is a separate and genuine candidate; the complex-transcendental NO applies only to mkl_umath.

metadata.expected_workflow: dtype coverage check per ufunc
metadata.why_it_matters: Complex-heavy DSP code is a common false positive for vectorized-math acceleration.

questions.text: A Monte Carlo simulation draws samples with `rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); rng.standard_normal(10_000_000)`. Will `mkl_random.patch_numpy_random()` accelerate it?
expected_topics: No. mkl_random patches only the legacy `np.random.*` functional API and the `np.random.RandomState` class. The modern `default_rng()`/`Generator` API is untouched.
Patching would have no effect on this code; the call site would need to change.

Acceleration requires changing the call site. Options: `mkl_random.interfaces.numpy_random.RandomState` (the documented drop-in for the legacy API, and what upstream's own deprecation warning points at), `mkl_random.MKLRandomState` when `brng`/`method` control is needed, or the patched legacy functional calls. All of them change the sampled values, since mkl_random is explicitly not fixed-seed compatible.

metadata.expected_workflow: API-surface check before recommending a patch
metadata.why_it_matters: The Generator API is now the NumPy default, so this NO is the most frequent real-world case.

questions.text: A codebase draws bulk samples via `np.random.standard_normal(size=50_000_000)` and its test suite asserts exact values for `np.random.seed(0)`. What should an agent recommend?
expected_topics: The sampling shape is what mkl_random's VSL backend targets: bulk legacy-API draws with a large `size`, filled per call with no size gate. No upstream benchmark quantifies the gain.
But patching changes the sampling sequence for the same seed, even with `brng='MT19937'`. It is not a fixed-seed drop-in, so the exact-value tests will fail.
The reproducibility hazard must be surfaced unprompted, and the patch requires an explicit OK from the user before being applied.

If the user drops to `mkl_random.MKLRandomState` directly, the `method` choice for normal sampling (ICDF / BoxMuller / BoxMuller2) is a third independent source of stream change. Note the patched `np.random.standard_normal` hardcodes `method='ICDF'` and does not expose the kwarg.

metadata.expected_workflow: fit check plus mandatory reproducibility caveat
metadata.why_it_matters: Silently changing a random stream under a fixed seed is the most damaging failure mode of these packages.

questions.text: An agent wants to confirm that `np.fft` is currently routing to MKL. It plans to check `mkl_fft.is_patched()`. Is that the right proof?
expected_topics: No. On an Intel-built numpy, FFT is already active while `is_patched()` still returns False, because that counter only tracks explicit patch calls.
The reliable proof is `np.fft.fft.__module__ == 'mkl_fft.interfaces._numpy_fft'`, which is true whether FFT is build-wired or explicitly patched.

Patching also re-exports the helpers, so `fftshift`, `fftfreq`, `rfftfreq`, and `ifftshift` start reporting `mkl_fft.interfaces._numpy_helper`. That is a re-export, not acceleration; judge only the transforms.

metadata.expected_workflow: runtime feature detection via bound-function __module__
metadata.why_it_matters: Using is_patched() for FFT produces false negatives on exactly the installs where FFT is already accelerated.

questions.text: `numpy.__config__.show()` indicates an MKL-backed build, but `threadpool_info()` called right after `import numpy` reports no entry with `internal_api: 'mkl'`. A colleague suggests running a matmul first and re-probing. Is that the right fix, and what should be investigated?
expected_topics: No, the warm-up call changes nothing. threadpoolctl enumerates shared libraries already loaded in the process image, and numpy's BLAS is a link-time dependency of its C extension module, so it is mapped at import before any BLAS call runs.
A missing `mkl` entry immediately after import is therefore genuine evidence, not a probe-ordering artifact. Investigate the link rather than the probe order.

Check what the extension module actually links against (`numpy.__config__.show()`, or `ldd`/`dumpbin` on `_multiarray_umath`). Real causes include MKL exposed under a filename threadpoolctl does not match, a BLAS shim, or MKL linked statically.
`mkl-service` is not involved: threadpoolctl declares no dependency on it and binds `mkl_rt` directly by symbol. Do not prescribe installing it to make the pool appear.

metadata.expected_workflow: BLAS call before reading threadpool_info
metadata.why_it_matters: Tests whether the agent knows library loading happens at import, so it neither dismisses real evidence nor prescribes a no-op warm-up call.

questions.text: A float32 audio pipeline calls `np.fft.rfft` under NumPy 2.x, and the team is considering `mkl_fft.interfaces.numpy_fft`. Some arrays are `np.longdouble`. What should be said about output dtype and extended precision?
expected_topics: For float32 there is no dtype change to flag. mkl_fft preserves single precision (`float32 -> complex64`), and since NumPy 2.0 stock `numpy.fft` also computes natively in float, double, or long double rather than always upcasting to double. The old 'NumPy upcasts float32' contrast applies only to NumPy 1.x.

Extended precision is where the real regression is. The numpy interface silently downcasts `longdouble -> float64` and `clongdouble -> complex128`; the source comment notes it downcasts rather than raising.
The scipy interface behaves differently on the same input: it raises `NotImplementedError` instead of downcasting silently. Naming that asymmetry is the useful part of the answer.
Since NumPy 2.0 supports longdouble FFT natively, routing this pipeline through mkl_fft is a precision regression for those arrays, not merely an absence of acceleration.

metadata.expected_workflow: dtype preservation check
metadata.why_it_matters: Guards against advice built on pre-NumPy-2.0 behaviour, and surfaces the silent-downcast versus raise asymmetry between the two interfaces.

questions.text: An environment has stock conda-forge numpy plus mkl_fft, mkl_random, and mkl_umath installed. A user reports 'no speedup at all' from FFT work. What is the most likely cause?
expected_topics: With a stock numpy the extensions stay dormant: `np.fft.*` still routes to `numpy.fft` until patching is enabled, via `mkl_fft.patch_numpy_fft()`, the `mkl_fft` context manager, or the CLI; alternatively call `mkl_fft.interfaces.numpy_fft` directly.

Confirm with `np.fft.fft.__module__`, which reads `numpy.fft` when dormant and `mkl_fft.interfaces._numpy_fft` when active. `mkl_fft.is_patched()` distinguishes an in-process or persistent `.pth` patch from an unwired environment.
The same conda command can land either an Intel-built or a conda-forge numpy depending on which channel wins, so determine the state at runtime rather than assuming.

Constraining BLAS does not wire numpy's FFT: `blas=*=mkl` on conda-forge, or `blas=*=*_intelmkl` on Intel's channel, only swaps the BLAS/LAPACK libraries. numpy's FFT is bundled pocketfft with no BLAS linkage, so it is wired by a Python-level rebinding (Intel's recipe patches `numpy/fft/__init__.py`) -- a different mechanism entirely.

metadata.expected_workflow: dormant-extension diagnosis
metadata.why_it_matters: This is the single most common reason an expected speedup does not appear.

questions.text: Code runs `np.floor_divide` and bitwise operations on large contiguous int64 arrays. Which of mkl_fft, mkl_random, or mkl_umath helps?
expected_topics: None. mkl_umath's VML paths are float, double, and complex; integer-only work is not covered.
Bitwise operations are not covered for any dtype.
The honest answer is that none of mkl_fft, mkl_random, or mkl_umath help this code.

Credit answers noting that integer typecodes appear in mkl_umath only as the `ldexp` exponent operand and `frexp` exponent output, never as a value dtype; and that mkl_random could only help generating such arrays, not operating on them.

metadata.expected_workflow: dtype and coverage check yielding an outright NO
metadata.why_it_matters: Tests whether the agent will state a complete NO rather than inventing a marginal benefit.

questions.text: An agent must decide whether `mkl_fft.interfaces.scipy_fft` is usable in the current environment. What check should it run, and what must it avoid?
expected_topics: Probe capability at runtime with `hasattr(mkl_fft.interfaces, 'scipy_fft')`.
Do not decide from a version string; use runtime feature detection.
`hasattr(mkl_fft, 'patch_numpy_fft')` similarly confirms the explicit-patch workflow is available.
The check is safe after a bare `import mkl_fft` because the package imports its `interfaces` submodule at top level.

The guard binds the submodule as an attribute (`from . import scipy_fft`) in the same success branch that appends to `__all__`, so `hasattr` is driven by attribute binding rather than `__all__` membership. When scipy or mkl-service is missing, `import mkl_fft` still succeeds and `hasattr` simply returns False.

metadata.expected_workflow: hasattr capability probe rather than version comparison
metadata.why_it_matters: Version-string gating breaks across the many release generations of these packages.

questions.text: A deployment check must confirm oneMKL FFT is actually in use. `mkl_fft.is_patched()` returns False, so the team reports that FFT is not accelerated. But on that machine `numpy.fft.fft` is already dispatching into mkl_fft. Reconcile the two.
expected_topics: `is_patched()` reports only the runtime monkeypatch installed by `patch_numpy_fft()`. It cannot see FFT wired in at build time by the NumPy distribution.
Check what the function actually is: `numpy.fft.fft.__module__` reads `mkl_fft.interfaces._numpy_fft` when routed and `numpy.fft` when not.
Measured on an Intel-distributed NumPy: `__module__` is `mkl_fft.interfaces._numpy_fft` while `mkl_fft.is_patched()` is False.
Control on stock conda-forge NumPy: `numpy.fft` with False, routed with True after `patch_numpy_fft()`, then both back after `restore_numpy_fft()`.
So `is_patched()` is sound evidence about the runtime patch and unsound evidence about activation. Do not answer the activation question with it.
The two extensions differ here. In that same environment `mkl_umath.is_patched()` was True, because that NumPy calls `patch_numpy_umath()` during its own import.

metadata.expected_workflow: prove activation from what the function actually is, rather than from a state flag that covers only one of the two activation paths
metadata.why_it_matters: Reporting 'not accelerated' for an environment that is already routed sends a team chasing a configuration problem that does not exist, and the flag they trusted is the documented one.
metadata.verified_by: executed in two environments: stock conda-forge numpy 2.4.3 with mkl_fft 2.3.2 gives np.fft.fft.__module__ 'numpy.fft' and is_patched() False, then 'mkl_fft.interfaces._numpy_fft' and True after patch_numpy_fft(), then both back after restore_numpy_fft(); Intel-distributed numpy 2.4.3 build py313h5623298_4 gives __module__ 'mkl_fft.interfaces._numpy_fft' with mkl_fft.is_patched() False while mkl_umath.is_patched() is True, the latter because that numpy's __init__.py calls patch_numpy_umath() at import (lines 937-946, file matched against its dist-info RECORD sha256)

questions.text: After `mkl_umath.patch_numpy_umath()`, a team checks whether VML is being reached by switching the VML accuracy mode from `ha` to `ep`. `np.sqrt` on a 50,000-element contiguous float64 array changes its results, so it is going through VML. `np.add` on the same two arrays shows no such sensitivity and no timing discontinuity anywhere in the sizes they sweep. Both are well past the 8192 threshold they read in the source. Explain precisely why.
expected_topics: Eligibility is per function class, not one global gate. `add`, `subtract` and `multiply` gate on a much higher constant than the transcendentals, and `divide` has its own.
The split is not algebraic versus transcendental: `sqrt`, `square`, `reciprocal`, `absolute`, `ceil`, `floor`, `fmax` and `fmin` all sit with the transcendentals.

The values are private `#define`s in `mkl_umath/src/mkl_umath_loops.c.src` and can change between releases. Read them at the tag matching the installed build rather than asserting a remembered number.
They cannot be recovered from an installed wheel: no `.c.src` ships, and no file under the package contains the string `THRESHOLD`.
The comparison is strictly greater-than at every dispatch site, so a size exactly equal to the threshold takes the fallback.
Which branch ran is not observable from Python. `MKL_VERBOSE` emits nothing for these ufuncs, and no NumPy ufunc attribute exposes the installed loop.
The one deterministic probe is a VML accuracy-mode differential via `mkl.vml_set_mode`, and it cannot settle `add`, `subtract` or `multiply`, which are single correctly-rounded operations.
Do not infer VML from a speedup; the non-VML fallback is already hand-vectorized. Eligibility also requires contiguous input.

metadata.expected_workflow: identify the per-function-class threshold rather than assuming one global gate
metadata.why_it_matters: Assuming a single 8192 gate leads to wrong capacity planning: elementwise add/sub/mul need 100k+ elements before VML engages at all.
metadata.verified_by: source read at mkl_umath/src/mkl_umath_loops.c.src lines 70, 71, 72 in upstream tag 0.4.1 (e41c869), which differs from master in this file by exactly one unrelated line (154, isinff -> isinf), so master line numbers are usable; grep confirmed 0 occurrences of ALGEBRAIC, 0 of '>= VML_', 19 of '> VML_' split as 8 ASM, 2 D, 9 TRANSCEDENTAL; every repeat block resolved to names, giving add/subtract and multiply at ASM (real and complex), divide alone at D, and sqrt/ceil/floor/fmax/fmin/absolute/reciprocal/square at TRANSCEDENTAL; confirmed the installed mkl_umath 0.4.1 wheel ships none of this (no src/, no .c.src, no THRESHOLD string anywhere under the package, none in SOURCES.txt or CMakeLists.txt); observability probed by execution: MKL_VERBOSE=1 and =2 silent for both ufuncs, np.sqrt.types/ntypes unchanged by patching, and a vml_set_mode ha-vs-ep differential bit-identical at n<=8192 and divergent from n=8193 (about 9.7e-11) for sqrt while insensitive for add at every size up to 300000; timing sweeps show a patched-only discontinuity at the sqrt gate and none at the add gate; 0.2.x traced via generate_umath.py at tags v0.1.5 and v0.2.0

questions.text: A parallel Monte Carlo harness assigns each of 8 workers its own MT2203 stream with `MKLRandomState(seed, brng=("MT2203", wid))` where `wid` comes from `np.arange(8)`. Results are reproducible and no warning is raised, but the variance across workers is exactly zero: all 8 workers return identical draws. What is happening?
expected_topics: All eight workers share one stream. `np.arange(8)` yields `np.int64`, and the member-selection branch honors the index only under `isinstance(s, int)`.
`np.int64` is not an `int` subclass, so the index is ignored and the stream id keeps its initial value of 0.
It is silent. The out-of-range warning never fires, because the value is not recognized as an integer at all.
Fix it at the call site with `int(wid)` or `operator.index(wid)`. Iterating `range(8)` also avoids it.
Verify independence by drawing from each worker's state and comparing, not from reproducibility, which holds either way.
Only MT2203 and WH are parametrized families. Every other BRNG has `stream_max == 1`, so the tuple form is meaningless for them.

metadata.expected_workflow: check the dtype of the stream index, not just the tuple syntax
metadata.why_it_matters: Silently collapsing N parallel streams onto one under-reports Monte Carlo variance while every surface signal (reproducible, no warning, correct API shape) looks healthy.
metadata.verified_by: executed against mkl_random 1.4.2: int64(5) draws == member 0 draws exactly, != member 5 draws, zero warnings under simplefilter('always'); 8 workers indexed by np.arange(8) give 1 distinct stream and a cross-worker mean std of exactly 0, against 8 distinct streams and std 0.0312 with range(8); int(wid) and operator.index(wid) both fix it; a Python int out of range does warn and wraps modulo smax (index 6030 warns and yields member 6, not member 0) while the np.int64 equivalent is silent; issubclass(np.int64, int) is False with no int in its MRO; stream_max verified behaviorally across all 11 BRNG tokens. Source read in the installed wheel, which does ship mklrand.pyx: _parse_brng_argument at mklrand.pyx:1513-1533 (stream_id initialized 0 at :1515, isinstance(s, int) gate at :1521, sole assignment at :1529), _brng_dict_stream_max at :1471-1483, and SIZE_OF_MT2203_FAMILY / SIZE_OF_WH_FAMILY at src/randomkit.cpp:122-123; _parse_brng_argument diffed byte-identical against upstream master

questions.text: A service calls `mkl_fft.patch_numpy_fft()` at startup and expects its `scipy.signal` convolution pipeline to run on oneMKL. The pipeline is unchanged. What did that patch actually cover, and what covers the rest?
expected_topics: `np.fft` and `scipy.fft` are independent surfaces. `patch_numpy_fft()` routes only `np.fft`; `scipy.fft` requires registering the backend separately.
Measured: after `patch_numpy_fft()`, `np.fft.fft.__module__` is `mkl_fft.interfaces._numpy_fft` while `scipy.fft` dispatched zero calls into the mkl backend.
The converse holds too. `scipy.fft.set_global_backend(mkl_fft.interfaces.scipy_fft)` routes `scipy.fft` and leaves `np.fft.fft.__module__` at `numpy.fft`.
`scipy.signal` does inherit the `scipy.fft` backend: `fftconvolve` dispatched two `rfftn` calls and one `irfftn` into it.
Instrument the entry point the caller actually uses. Real-input convolution never calls `fft`, so watching `fft` alone reports a false negative.
Only the `scipy_fft` namespace carries `set_workers`/`get_workers`, so the numpy-patch route provides no thread knob at all.

metadata.expected_workflow: identify which activation surface a given call path reads, instead of assuming one patch covers the whole process
metadata.why_it_matters: Half-activated stacks are the common production outcome: the NumPy path is accelerated, the SciPy path silently is not, and the thread knob exists on only one of them.
metadata.verified_by: executed against mkl_fft 2.3.2 + scipy 1.17.1 with a spy wrapping all 14 backend entry points: after patch_numpy_fft() np.fft.fft.__module__ is 'mkl_fft.interfaces._numpy_fft' and scipy.fft produced 0 backend dispatches; after scipy.fft.set_global_backend(interfaces.scipy_fft) scipy.fft.fft produced 1 dispatch, np.fft.fft produced 0, and np.fft.fft.__module__ was still 'numpy.fft'; scipy.signal.fftconvolve dispatched rfftn twice and irfftn once, and scipy.signal.convolve(method='fft') the same; a spy watching only 'fft' reported 0 dispatches for fftconvolve, which is why the entry point matters; set_workers/get_workers present only on interfaces.scipy_fft per dir() across all three namespaces

questions.text: A team wants non-overlapping mkl_random streams per worker and plans to call `leapfrog(k, nstreams)` on an MT2203 generator, having read that leapfrog partitions a stream into interleaved subsequences. Will that work, and what should they use?
expected_topics: No. `leapfrog` raises `ValueError` on MT2203; across every BRNG the package exposes, it succeeds only for WH, MCG31 and MCG59.
`skipahead` is supported far more broadly and does work on MT2203, including on non-zero family members.
Support is per BRNG and must be probed at runtime. `hasattr` is True for every BRNG, so the check has to invoke the method and catch the error.
The documented support matrix is not a safe substitute; at the time of writing it omitted MT2203 from the skipahead list.
For MT2203 the idiomatic mechanism is family-member selection via `brng=("MT2203", member)`.
With `skipahead`, copy each worker's state after its jump and keep each worker under `nskips` draws, or the streams overlap.
Neither method exists on `mkl_random.interfaces.numpy_random.RandomState`, which subclasses the private base and defines neither.

metadata.expected_workflow: check per-BRNG method support at runtime instead of assuming uniform support or trusting the doc matrix
metadata.why_it_matters: Choosing the wrong partitioning primitive fails loudly, but the documented support matrix understates skipahead, so a doc-driven answer needlessly rejects the primitive that works.
metadata.verified_by: executed against mkl_random 1.4.2 across all 11 BRNG tokens enumerated from _brng_dict at mklrand.pyx:1455-1469: leapfrog OK only WH/MCG31/MCG59; skipahead OK for 9 including MT2203 and non-zero MT2203 members, ValueError for R250 and NONDETERM; upstream docs/source/how_to.rst skipahead list omits MT2203 while its leapfrog list is exact, and no other docs/source page states support for either method; VSL_RNG_ERROR_{LEAPFROG,SKIPAHEAD}_UNSUPPORTED translation read at src/randomkit.cpp:305-328 plus mklrand.pyx:6737-6766; class placement read at mklrand.pyx:1546/6670/6725/6746/7076 and interfaces/_numpy_random.py:34-35; nskips constraint quoted from how_to.rst and demonstrated in examples/parallel_random_states.py

questions.text: Code ported from SciPy calls `mkl_fft.interfaces.scipy_fft.fft(x, n=16, overwrite_x=True)` on an 8-element complex128 array to zero-pad in place. Under SciPy this worked; under the mkl_fft backend it raises. Why, and what is the correct fix?
expected_topics: `overwrite_x` and a length-changing `n` or `s` are mutually exclusive. In-place only makes sense when the output shape equals the input shape.
It raises a `ValueError` naming the expected and received output shapes, which points at a shape rather than at the offending keyword.
Mechanism: the input is passed as `out` whenever `overwrite_x` is set and the dtype is complex, without consulting `n` or `s`, and out-array validation then rejects the shape.
The fix is to drop `overwrite_x` whenever the transform length changes. Truncating fails the same way as padding.
It is honored only for complex dtypes. Real input is silently left unmodified and a new complex array is returned.
Every real and Hermitian transform ignores it as well, and most carry a source comment saying so.
`overwrite_x` does not exist on the top-level `mkl_fft` API, which takes `out` instead. Only `interfaces.scipy_fft` accepts it.

metadata.expected_workflow: recognize that in-place and length-changing arguments are mutually exclusive here
metadata.why_it_matters: A drop-in SciPy backend that raises on a valid SciPy call breaks ported code at runtime, and the message names a shape rather than the offending keyword.
metadata.verified_by: executed against mkl_fft 2.3.2 + scipy 1.17.1: mkl raises 'ValueError: output array has wrong shape, expected ((16,)) got ((8,)).' on n=16 with overwrite_x, both directly and through scipy.fft.set_backend, while n=4 raises the truncating equivalent and n=8 or n=None succeed and plain scipy returns len 16; complex input confirmed reused in place by identity (r is x, np.shares_memory True, input buffer modified) rather than by absence of an error, and float64/float32 input confirmed unmodified with a new complex array returned; traceback frames _scipy_fft.py:251 -> _mkl_fft.py:54 -> _pydfti.pyx:467 -> _pydfti.pyx:356; source read at interfaces/_scipy_fft.py:220-225 (_use_input_as_out, which takes no n or s parameter) and upstream _pydfti.pyx:347-360 (_validate_out_array, compiled in the installed build so no installed file:line exists); 8 occurrences of the '# Note: overwrite_x is not utilized' comment at _scipy_fft.py 388/405/484/509/530/548/634/660 with the four 2-D wrappers ignoring it uncommented; removal recorded in upstream CHANGELOG.md '## [2.1.0] - 2025-10-06' / '### Changed' as 'Dropped support for overwrite_x parameter in mkl_fft [gh-185]', whose PR body states the out kwarg made it redundant

questions.text: A library calls `mkl_umath.patch_numpy_umath()` in its module import and again in a helper, then calls `restore_numpy_umath()` once in a teardown hook and asserts NumPy is unpatched. The assertion fails. Explain the semantics.
expected_topics: Patching is reference counted. Two `patch_numpy_umath()` calls raise the counter to 2, and one `restore_numpy_umath()` decrements to 1 without unpatching.
Upstream encodes exactly this sequence in `mkl_umath/tests/test_patching.py::test_patch_redundant_patching`.
Restoring more times than patching does not raise. It emits a `RuntimeWarning` and returns without unpatching, and that balance check is thread-local.
The patch swaps C loop pointers inside NumPy's existing ufunc objects, so `np.sin is np.sin` holds and you cannot detect it by inspecting Python objects.
Use the `mkl_umath.mkl_umath` context manager or decorator for balanced lifetimes; it is reentrant over the same counter.
Upstream recommends it specifically for multi-threaded programs, not unconditionally.
Do not assume the counter starts at zero. Some NumPy distributions call `patch_numpy_umath()` during their own import, which makes your first patch the second.

metadata.expected_workflow: reason about reference-counted patch state rather than assuming a boolean toggle

questions.text: A service registers the mkl_fft SciPy backend, then wraps its transforms in `with scipy.fft.set_workers(2):` to limit oversubscription inside an outer process pool. Thread usage does not drop. Why, and how should thread count actually be controlled?
expected_topics: `scipy.fft.set_workers` never reaches the mkl backend. The uarray dispatch forwards no `workers` entry, so the backend silently applies its own default.
An explicit per-call `scipy.fft.fft(x, workers=n)` does forward.
The backend default is `mkl.get_max_threads()`, not SciPy's 1. Inside an outer process pool that default is the oversubscription source.
Use `mkl_fft.interfaces.scipy_fft.set_workers(n)` as a context manager, or pass `workers=n` on each call.
`MKL_NUM_THREADS` is latched by the MKL runtime when it loads, so setting it in-process afterwards is invisible even to `mkl.get_max_threads()`.
Separately, the backend caches the thread count per context on first access, so a later `mkl.set_num_threads()` does not move `get_workers()`.
The scope does not reach `threading.Thread` children. A fresh thread re-runs the lazy initializer rather than inheriting the scoped value.
Quote no absolute thread count; it is host-specific. The invariants are `get_workers() == mkl.get_max_threads()` and `scipy.fft.get_workers() == 1`.

questions.text: A pricing model calls `MKLRandomState(seed).standard_normal(n, method="BOXMULLER")` to select the Box-Muller sampler. Output is reproducible and no warning appears, but a colleague says the method argument is not taking effect. Who is right, and how would you check?
expected_topics: The colleague is right. The accepted alias is `"BoxMuller"` and the lookup is case-sensitive, so `"BOXMULLER"` is not recognized.
An unrecognized `method` is silently swallowed and the default is used, with no warning and no exception.
Verify by differential testing: draw with the intended method and with the default from the same seed and assert the vectors differ.
Contrast `brng`, which is case-insensitive and does warn on an unrecognized value before falling back to MT19937.
Five distributions accept `method=` and they do not all act on it. `standard_normal` honors it while `lognormal` ignores it entirely.
`lognormal` is a different failure from the alias miss: its alias resolves and a separate entry point runs, so the no-op sits below the Python layer.
The docstrings advertise tokens such as `mkl_random.ICDF`, but that attribute does not exist. The exact-cased strings are the working path.

questions.text: A team upgrading mkl_umath needs to know whether `np.maximum` on float64 is still accelerated in the build they now have. They compare `np.maximum.types` before and after patching, see no difference, and conclude the patch did not apply. Is that conclusion sound, and how should they check?
expected_topics: No. NumPy ufunc introspection cannot report mkl_umath coverage at all.
`PyUFunc_ReplaceLoopBySignature` swaps the C loop pointer for an existing signature and leaves the signature table untouched.
Measured: `np.maximum.types`, `np.sqrt.types` and both `ntypes` are identical before and after `patch_numpy_umath()`.
Object identity is no evidence either. `np.sin is np.sin` still holds and `np.sin.__module__` stays `numpy`.
Check the extension instead: membership in `mkl_umath.__all__` or `dir(mkl_umath._ufuncs)`, since the covered set changes between releases.
Do not infer coverage from a speedup. The non-VML fallback loop is itself faster than stock NumPy at some sizes.

metadata.why_it_matters: Both halves of the naive check fail silently: the ufunc looks untouched whether or not the patch applied, so a team can conclude either way and be wrong.
